### 00-overview.md
# Boldteq Software Factory — Master Overview

This document is the single source of truth for the entire Boldteq Software Factory system. If you have lost everything and are starting from scratch, start here, then follow the numbered docs in order.

---

## What Is This System?

The Boldteq Software Factory is a local AI-powered development infrastructure that runs on your Mac. It turns Claude Code (the VS Code extension) from a general-purpose assistant into a coordinated team of 12 specialist agents that know your stack, your standards, and your active projects.

Every component in this system has one job. They are designed to work together without requiring you to repeat context.

---

## The Five Components

### 1. Claude Hub — The Control Center

**Location:** `/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/`

Claude Hub is a local web application running on `http://localhost:3847`. It has two parts:

- **Express backend** (`src/server.js`) — REST API that reads/writes agent files, CLAUDE.md files, slash commands, and handles orchestration runs and playground agent calls.
- **React/TypeScript/Vite frontend** (`client/`) — The browser dashboard you use to manage everything.

Claude Hub is kept alive 24/7 by pm2 and auto-starts on macOS login via a LaunchAgent. You never manually start it.

Pages in the dashboard:
- **Dashboard** — overview of all projects, agents, and commands
- **All Agents** — browse and edit all 12 global agents
- **All Commands** — browse slash commands across all projects
- **Orchestration** — visual DAG workflow builder for chaining agents
- **Playground** — test any single agent interactively
- **Global CLAUDE.md** — view and edit the global instruction file
- **Project Detail** — per-project agents, commands, and CLAUDE.md
- **Setup & Status** — system health, SDK installer, project directories
- **Settings** — project directory configuration

### 2. Global CLAUDE.md — The Briefing File

**Location:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`

Every single Claude Code session in every project reads this file first. It contains the Boldteq identity, build standards, agent routing rules, and active project list. It is the foundation that makes Claude Code behave consistently across all projects. Without it, Claude Code has no knowledge of your stack, agents, or standards.

### 3. The Agent Roster — The Specialist Team

**Location:** `~/.claude/agents/`

12 `.md` files, each one a specialist persona with a name, model, and system prompt. Claude Code loads all of them at startup and can route tasks to the right specialist automatically. You can also invoke them explicitly by name. The agents cover the entire build lifecycle from research to deployment to monitoring.

### 4. The SDK — Programmatic Agent Access

**Location:** `claude-hub/sdk/` (installed as `@boldteq/agents` in each project)

A tiny Node.js package that lets any project call any agent over HTTP with one line of code. It posts to Claude Hub which runs `claude -p` with the agent's instructions and streams back the result. Zero cost beyond the existing Claude subscription.

### 5. Slash Commands — Repeatable Workflows

**Location:** `[project]/.claude/commands/`

`.md` files that become `/commandname` shortcuts in Claude Code chat. Pinzo has `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review`, and `/db`. These are pre-written, detailed instructions for the most common workflows in that project. You type the command, pass arguments, and Claude Code executes the full workflow.

### 01-setup.md
# Claude Hub — Complete Setup Guide

This guide walks you through setting up the entire Claude Hub system from zero. By the end, Claude Hub will be running permanently in the background, auto-starting on every login, and all 12 agents will be available in every Claude Code session.

If any step fails, jump to the TROUBLESHOOTING section at the bottom.

---

## Prerequisites

### Why each prerequisite matters

Before installing anything, verify that the right versions are present. The system has been tested and runs on these specific versions. Older versions may work but are not guaranteed.

### Node.js 20+

Claude Hub's backend is a Node.js Express server. The `@boldteq/agents` SDK uses the native `fetch` API which requires Node 18+. The current setup uses **Node 20.20.1 via nvm**.

```bash
node --version
```

Expected output:
```
v20.20.1
```

If not installed or wrong version:

```bash
# Install nvm (Node Version Manager)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash

# Reload shell
source ~/.zshrc

# Install Node 20
nvm install 20
nvm use 20
nvm alias default 20

# Verify
node --version
# v20.x.x
```

📝 When you install Node via nvm, the binary lives at `~/.nvm/versions/node/v20.x.x/bin/node`. This exact path is used in the LaunchAgent plist. If you change Node versions later, you must update the plist.

### npm 9+

Ships automatically with Node 18+. Verify:

```bash
npm --version
```

Expected output:
```
10.8.2
```

No manual installation needed if Node is correct.

### pm2 (Process Manager)

pm2 keeps Claude Hub running permanently even after closing your terminal. It restarts the process if it crashes, and persists the process list across reboots.

```bash
npm install -g pm2
pm2 --version
```

Expected output:
```
6.0.14
```

If not installed:
```bash
npm install -g pm2
```

📝 The `-g` flag installs pm2 globally so it's accessible from any directory and as a system command.

### Claude Code (CLI)

Claude Hub calls the `claude` CLI to run agents. This must be installed and authenticated.

```bash
claude --version
```

Expected output (something like):
```
Claude Code 1.x.x
```

If not installed, go to https://claude.ai/code and follow the installation instructions. After installing, authenticate:

```bash
claude login
```

⚠️ Claude Hub will not be able to run agents (Playground, Orchestration) if `claude` is not authenticated. The dashboard itself will still work.

---

## Step 1 — Verify the Claude Hub Directory

Why this matters: Claude Hub must live at a specific absolute path because that path is hardcoded in `ecosystem.config.js` and the LaunchAgent plist. Moving it after setup requires updating those files.

```bash
ls "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/"
```

Expected output:
```

ORCHESTRATION_GUIDE.md
README.md
client/
config.json
docs/
ecosystem.config.js
node_modules/
orchestrations.json
package.json
package-lock.json

```

Key files to confirm exist:
- `src/server.js` — the backend
- `ecosystem.config.js` — pm2 configuration
- `sdk/` — the @boldteq/agents package
- `client/` — the React frontend source
- `public-dist/` — the built frontend (served by Express)

⚠️ If `public-dist/` is missing or empty, the frontend won't load. See Step 3 for how to build it.

### Checking ecosystem.config.js

This file tells pm2 how to run Claude Hub. Read it:

```bash
cat "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/ecosystem.config.js"
```

Expected content:
```javascript
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: 'claude-hub',
      script: './src/server.js',
      cwd: '/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub',
      interpreter: 'node',
      watch: false,
      autorestart: true,
      max_restarts: 5,
      env: {
        NODE_ENV: 'production',
        PORT: 3847,
      },
      error_file: '/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-error.log',
      out_file: '/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-out.log',
      log_date_format: 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss',
    },
  ],
}
```

Each field explained:
- `name: 'claude-hub'` — the pm2 process name. Used in all pm2 commands.
- `script: './src/server.js'` — the entry point, relative to `cwd`.
- `cwd: '/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub'` — absolute working directory. If Claude Hub moves, update this.
- `watch: false` — do not auto-restart when files change (important for production stability).
- `autorestart: true` — restart automatically if the process crashes.
- `max_restarts: 5` — stop restarting after 5 consecutive crashes (prevents infinite crash loops).
- `PORT: 3847` — Claude Hub listens on this port. All SDK calls and browser access use this port.
- `error_file` / `out_file` — log files. View with `pm2 logs claude-hub`.

⚠️ If you are on a different Mac or different username, update the `cwd` path to match your actual home directory.

## Step 4 — Set Up pm2 (Permanent Background Service)

### Why pm2?

Without pm2, Claude Hub only runs while your terminal is open. Close the terminal → Claude Hub stops → SDK calls fail → Playground stops working → Orchestration stops working.

pm2 is a process manager that:
- Runs Claude Hub as a background daemon (no terminal needed)
- Automatically restarts it if it crashes
- Persists across terminal sessions
- Starts automatically after a system reboot (when combined with LaunchAgent)
- Gives you logging, monitoring, and process control

### Start Claude Hub with pm2

```bash
cd "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub"
pm2 start ecosystem.config.js
```

Expected output:
```
[PM2] Applying action restartProcessId on app [claude-hub](ids: [ 0 ])
[PM2] [claude-hub](0) ✓
┌────┬───────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────┬────────┬──────┬───────────┬──────────┬──────────┐

├────┼───────────────┼─────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼──────────┼────────┼──────┼───────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
│ 0  │ claude-hub    │ default     │ 1.0.0   │ fork    │ 97206    │ 0s     │ 0    │ online    │ 0%       │ 44.6mb   │

The `status` column must show `online`. If it shows `errored`, see TROUBLESHOOTING below.

### Save the pm2 process list

This tells pm2 to remember this process. Without saving, pm2 forgets the process after a reboot.

```bash
pm2 save
```

Expected output:
```

[PM2] Successfully saved in /Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/dump.pm2
```

### Verify it's running

```bash
pm2 status
```

Look for `claude-hub` with status `online`. The `↺` (restart) counter should be 0 or very low. If it's climbing rapidly (10, 20, 30...) the process is crash-looping — check logs.

### Check logs

```bash
pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 20
```

Expected output includes:
```

```

No error lines like `Error:`, `EADDRINUSE`, `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, etc.

### The full set of pm2 commands you will use

```bash
pm2 status                    # Show all processes and their status
pm2 restart claude-hub        # Restart after making changes to server.js
pm2 stop claude-hub           # Stop Claude Hub (it stays in pm2's list)
pm2 start claude-hub          # Start it again after stopping
pm2 delete claude-hub         # Remove from pm2 entirely
pm2 logs claude-hub           # Stream live logs
pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 50  # Show last 50 lines
pm2 flush claude-hub          # Clear the log files
pm2 monit                     # Interactive monitor (CPU, memory, logs)
pm2 list                      # Alias for pm2 status
```

📝 `pm2 restart` is what you run after editing `src/server.js`. The process restarts with the new code. You do not need to `pm2 delete` and re-add it.

## Step 5 — LaunchAgent Setup (Auto-Start on macOS Login)

### Why a LaunchAgent?

pm2 manages the process, but pm2 itself needs to be started after a reboot. The LaunchAgent is macOS's built-in service system. It runs a specified program when you log in, before you open any apps.

Without a LaunchAgent:
- After a Mac restart, pm2 is not running
- Claude Hub is not running
- The SDK fails silently in all projects
- You must manually run `pm2 resurrect` or `pm2 start ecosystem.config.js` after every reboot

With the LaunchAgent:
- Mac restarts → login → LaunchAgent fires → `node src/server.js` starts → Claude Hub is running → all SDK calls work

📝 Note: The LaunchAgent in this setup runs Claude Hub **directly** (not via pm2). This is intentional — it guarantees Claude Hub starts even if pm2's process list was lost.

### Check if the plist already exists

```bash
ls ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist
```

Expected: path printed (file exists).

If missing, you need to create it. See "Creating the plist from scratch" below.

### The full plist content

The file at `~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist` should contain:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>io.boldteq.claude-hub</string>

  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin/node</string>
    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/src/server.js</string>
  </array>

  <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub</string>

  <key>RunAtLoad</key>
  <true/>

  <key>KeepAlive</key>
  <true/>

  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-launchd.log</string>

  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>

**Symptom:** `npm start` fails with `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3847`

**Cause:** Another process is using port 3847. Either a previous Claude Hub instance is still running, or something else claimed the port.

**Fix:**
```bash
# Find what's using the port
lsof -ti:3847

# If it returns a PID, kill it
kill -9 $(lsof -ti:3847)

# Now start Claude Hub
pm2 restart claude-hub
# or
npm start
```

### 02-agents.md
# Claude Code Agents — Complete Reference

This document covers everything about the 12 global agents: what they are, how Claude Code discovers them, how to invoke them, how to create new ones, and how to maintain them.

---

## What Are Agents?

An agent is a `.md` file with YAML frontmatter that defines a specialist persona for Claude Code. When Claude Code runs an agent, it reads the file's frontmatter for metadata and uses the file body as the system prompt for that Claude call.

Agents solve a specific problem: instead of explaining your entire stack and standards to Claude on every task, you write that context once in the agent file. From then on, invoking `koda` means "use this pre-loaded context about our Shopify stack and feature-building standards."

They also allow automatic routing — Claude Code reads all agent `description` fields and can route a task to the right specialist without you explicitly naming one.

---

## How Claude Code Discovers Agents

Claude Code reads all `.md` files in these directories at startup:

1. `~/.claude/agents/` — global agents, available in every project
2. `[project]/.claude/agents/` — project-level agents, available only in that project

No registration or configuration needed. Drop a `.md` file into either directory and it is immediately available in the next Claude Code session.

📝 Claude Code loads agents at session start, not on every message. If you create or edit an agent file, open a new chat window to pick up the changes.

### File Naming

The filename (without `.md`) becomes the agent's slug — the name you use to call it programmatically:
- `koda.md` → invoked as `koda`
- `nova.md` → invoked as `nova`
- `custom-specialist.md` → invoked as `custom-specialist`

Names must match the regex `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+`. No spaces, no special characters.

### Global vs Project-Level Agents

| Scope | Directory | Available in |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| Global | `~/.claude/agents/` | Every Claude Code session, every project |
| Project | `[project]/.claude/agents/` | Only when that project is open |

Project-level agents override global agents with the same filename. If `~/.claude/agents/koda.md` and `Pinzo/.claude/agents/koda.md` both exist, Pinzo's version takes priority when working in Pinzo. This lets you specialize a global agent for one project without affecting others.

**When to use project-level agents:**
- A workflow is too specific to one project to belong globally (e.g., a Pinzo widget specialist)
- You want to override a global agent with project-specific context
- A project has a unique tech stack that doesn't apply anywhere else

**When to keep it global:**
- The agent's skills apply to all projects (most agents should be global)
- You want Rex to be able to route to this agent from any project

---

## The 12 Global Agents

These agents cover the entire build lifecycle. They are the "team" that executes work while you make decisions.

### Rex — Commander

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| File | `~/.claude/agents/rex.md` |
| Model | opus |
| Purpose | Master orchestrator. Entry point for any new project or sprint. |

Rex owns outcomes, not tasks. Give Rex a brief (one line or ten) and it coordinates the full agent team in the correct order. It does not write code, research, or design — it sequences, delegates, and enforces quality gates.

Rex operates in four modes:
- **Mode A (New Product Build):** Nova → Arya → Riko → Koda → Luna → Sage → Bolt → Mira
- **Mode B (Feature Addition):** Arya → Koda → Luna → Sage → Bolt → Mira
- **Mode C (Maintenance/Fix):** Vex → Koda → Luna → Sage → Bolt
- **Mode D (Launch/Go-Live):** Sage → Quill → Bolt → Hawk

**Typical inputs:** Product brief, feature request, "fix sprint for Pinzo", "prepare Rankora for launch"
**Typical outputs:** Coordinated execution plan, dispatches to specialist agents in order
**When NOT to use:** When you already know which specialist you need. Don't route to Rex if you just want Koda to build one component.

---

### Nova — Market Research

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| File | `~/.claude/agents/nova.md` |
| Model | sonnet |
| Purpose | Competitive intelligence before building anything new. |

Nova researches competitors, extracts pricing patterns, identifies table stakes features, and finds USP opportunities. Run Nova before any new product build. Its output feeds into Arya's architecture.

**Typical inputs:** "Research AI resume screening tools — top 5 competitors", "What are the top Shopify size chart apps and what do they all have?"
**Typical outputs:** Competitor table with names/features/pricing, weak points, USP gap, V1 recommendations
**When NOT to use:** Mid-build when the architecture is already decided. Nova is a pre-build agent.

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| File | `~/.claude/agents/arya.md` |
| Model | opus |
| Purpose | Stack selection, data model, API design, sprint planning. |

Arya converts Nova's research and your brief into a buildable plan. It selects the stack, defines the data model, designs auth and billing strategy, scopes V1, and creates the sprint plan. For Mode B (feature addition), Arya scopes the change only — no full redesign.

**Typical inputs:** Nova's research output, product brief, constraints (e.g., "must use Shopify billing API")
**Typical outputs:** Stack decision, data model (entities + relations), API routes, V1 scope, sprint order
**When NOT to use:** For small bug fixes or isolated changes that don't affect architecture.

### Riko — Project Setup

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| File | `~/.claude/agents/riko.md` |
| Model | sonnet |
| Purpose | Scaffolds a runnable project from Arya's plan. |

Riko handles everything needed to get from "Arya's architecture document" to "a running project with all boilerplate in place." This includes: folder structure, configs, auth boilerplate, billing boilerplate, CI/CD, error tracking (Sentry), and seed data.

**Typical inputs:** Arya's complete architecture document, stack choice
**Typical outputs:** A complete project scaffold that compiles and runs with auth and billing wired up

| Field | Value |

| File | `~/.claude/agents/koda.md` |
| Model | sonnet |
| Purpose | All production code — frontend, backend, database, integrations. |

Koda is the primary builder. It reads CLAUDE.md and memory first, matches existing code patterns, and delivers complete, production-grade features. It builds types first, then database, then API, then UI. It never skips quality gates.

**Typical inputs:** Feature specification from Arya's sprint plan, file paths to reference, stack context
**Typical outputs:** Complete implementation across all layers, typecheck passes, empty states and loading states included
**When NOT to use:** For diagnostics or debugging. Route bugs to Vex first for diagnosis, then Koda for the fix.

Vex has a built-in error encyclopedia covering Supabase, Stripe, Shopify, React Router, Prisma, and AI SDK errors. It classifies bugs by category (auth, TypeScript, Polaris, DB, Shopify API, webhooks, billing) and diagnoses root causes before fixing.

**Typical inputs:** Error message with stack trace, file path where error occurs, "build is failing on typecheck"
**Typical outputs:** Root cause diagnosis, minimal targeted fix, verification steps

**Typical inputs:** "Write tests for the ZIP code check API endpoint", "Test the subscription billing flow"

### Frontmatter fields

|-------|----------|--------|-------|

| `description` | Yes | Any string | Used for auto-routing — be precise |
| `model` | Yes | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku` | Affects cost and quality |
| `tools` | No | Comma-separated tool names | Restricts available tools |

### Model selection guide

| Model | Speed | Cost | Use for |
|-------|-------|------|---------|
| `haiku` | Fastest | Lowest | Simple tasks: formatting, classification, simple transforms |
| `sonnet` | Fast | Medium | Most agents — code generation, research, content writing |

The `description` field is what Claude Code reads to decide which agent handles a task. Bad descriptions lead to wrong routing.

The good description includes: what it does, in what context, what kinds of tasks, and any notable specializations.

## Agent Quality Tips

### What makes agent instructions good

1. **Clear identity** — the agent knows exactly who it is and what its scope is
2. **Explicit non-responsibilities** — saying "you do NOT write tests" is as important as saying what it does do
3. **Concrete patterns** — "use `upsert` for singleton records" beats "handle data correctly"
4. **Output format specified** — the agent knows what shape to return results in
5. **Quality gates explicit** — the agent knows what "done" means

### What makes agent instructions bad

1. **Too broad** — "help with any code task" gives no routing signal
2. **Missing context** — agent doesn't know the stack, framework versions, or project structure
3. **No scope boundary** — agent will attempt everything instead of knowing when to hand off
4. **Ambiguous instructions** — "handle errors properly" vs "wrap every action in try/catch and return `{ error: msg }` with status 500"
5. **No output format** — agent returns different structures on every call

### The "one clear responsibility" rule

Each agent should be able to answer "what is the one thing you are the expert on?" in one sentence. If the answer requires "and also...", split into multiple agents or make the description more specific.

Koda builds features. Vex fixes bugs. Luna tests. Sage reviews. They do not step on each other's territory because their scope boundaries are explicit in their files.

# @boldteq/agents SDK — Complete Reference

This document covers the `@boldteq/agents` SDK: what it is, how it works internally, how to install it in a new project, and the full API reference with examples.

---

## What the SDK Is and the Problem It Solves

Every Boldteq project occasionally needs to call a Claude agent programmatically — not just interactively from a chat window. Examples:

- An API route in Rankora that calls Quill to generate a job description summary
- A Pinzo webhook handler that calls Vex to diagnose an error and log the diagnosis
- A build script that calls Nova to research a competitor before a planning session
- An admin dashboard action that calls Koda to auto-generate code suggestions

Without the SDK, doing this requires: knowing the `claude` CLI syntax, managing subprocesses, parsing SSE output, handling timeouts, and writing error handling from scratch — every time, in every project.

The SDK wraps all of that into a single function:

```javascript
const result = await callAgent('quill', 'Write App Store listing for Pinzo')
```

That's it. One line. The SDK handles the HTTP call to Claude Hub, which handles the `claude -p` subprocess, SSE streaming, and response parsing. The result comes back as a structured object.

---

## Architecture: How a Call Actually Works

```
Your code calls:
callAgent('quill', 'Write listing for Pinzo')
  │
  ▼
SDK (sdk/index.js)
  POST http://localhost:3847/api/playground/run
  Body: { agentName: 'quill', prompt: 'Write listing...' }
  │
  ▼
Claude Hub backend (src/server.js)
  1. Reads ~/.claude/agents/quill.md
  2. Extracts the agent's system prompt (body after frontmatter)
  3. Constructs: claude -p "[system prompt]\n\n[user prompt]"
  4. Spawns the subprocess
  5. Streams output back as Server-Sent Events (SSE)
  │
  ▼
SDK parses the SSE stream:
  - Looks for { type: 'done', output: '...' }
  - Or { type: 'error', error: '...' }
  │
  ▼
Returns to your code:
  { success: true, output: '...the agent response...', agent: 'quill' }
  or
  { success: false, output: '', agent: 'quill', error: 'reason' }
```

Key characteristics:
- **Zero additional cost** — uses your existing Claude subscription. The `claude -p` subprocess runs under the same authenticated account as your interactive Claude Code sessions.
- **Synchronous from your code's perspective** — `await callAgent(...)` blocks until the agent completes or times out.
- **Never throws** — the SDK catches all errors internally and returns them in the `error` field. Your code never needs a try/catch around `callAgent`.
- **Requires Claude Hub running** — if `http://localhost:3847` is not reachable, the call fails immediately with a "not reachable" error message.

```javascript
/**
 * @boldteq/agents
 * Call any global Claude agent from any Boldteq app.
 * Claude Hub must be running (auto-starts on login via LaunchAgent).
 */

const CLAUDE_HUB_URL = process.env.CLAUDE_HUB_URL || 'http://localhost:3847'

/**
 * Call a global agent with a prompt.
 * @param {string} agentName - e.g. "quill", "vex", "nova", "sage", "koda"
 * @param {string} prompt - the task to send
 * @param {number} [timeoutMs=120000] - timeout in ms
 * @returns {Promise<{ success: boolean, output: string, agent: string, error?: string }>}
 */
async function callAgent(agentName, prompt, timeoutMs = 120000) {
  const controller = new AbortController()
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs)

  try {
    const response = await fetch(`${CLAUDE_HUB_URL}/api/playground/run`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ agentName, prompt }),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })

    clearTimeout(timeout)

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Claude Hub returned ${response.status}`)
    }

    const text = await response.text()
    const events = text
      .split('\n')
      .filter(line => line.startsWith('data: '))
      .map(line => { try { return JSON.parse(line.slice(6)) } catch { return null } })
      .filter(Boolean)

    const errorEvent = events.find(e => e.type === 'error')
    if (errorEvent) return { success: false, output: '', agent: agentName, error: errorEvent.error }

    const doneEvent = events.find(e => e.type === 'done' || e.type === 'complete')
    return { success: true, output: doneEvent?.output || '', agent: agentName }

  } catch (err) {
    clearTimeout(timeout)
    const msg = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)
    return {
      success: false,
      output: '',
      agent: agentName,
      error: msg.includes('abort')
        ? `Timed out after ${timeoutMs / 1000}s`
        : `Claude Hub not reachable at ${CLAUDE_HUB_URL} — is it running?`,
    }
  }
}

/**
 * List all available global agents.
 * @returns {Promise<Array<{ filename, name, description, model, body }>>}
 */
async function listAgents() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`${CLAUDE_HUB_URL}/api/global/agents`)
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`)
    return await res.json()
  } catch {
    return []
  }
}

/**
 * Check if Claude Hub is reachable.
 * @returns {Promise<boolean>}
 */
async function isOnline() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`${CLAUDE_HUB_URL}/api/global/agents`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) })
    return res.ok
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

module.exports = { callAgent, listAgents, isOnline }
```

## Full API Reference

### `callAgent(agentName, prompt, timeoutMs?)`

The primary function. Calls any global agent with a task and waits for the response.

**Parameters:**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `agentName` | `string` | Yes | — | Agent filename without `.md`. Must match a file in `~/.claude/agents/`. Example: `'koda'`, `'quill'`, `'nova'` |
| `prompt` | `string` | Yes | — | The task or instruction to send to the agent. Write it as you would write a message to that specialist. |
| `timeoutMs` | `number` | No | `120000` | Maximum time to wait in milliseconds. Default is 2 minutes. Increase for complex tasks. |

**Returns:** `Promise<AgentResult>`

```typescript
interface AgentResult {
  success: boolean   // true if the agent ran and returned output
  output: string     // the agent's full response text (empty string if success is false)
  agent: string      // the agentName that was called (echoed back)
  error?: string     // error message (only set if success is false)
}
```

**Examples:**

```javascript
// Basic call
const result = await callAgent('quill', 'Write a tagline for Pinzo')
if (result.success) {
  console.log(result.output)
} else {
  console.error(result.error)
}

// With custom timeout for a long task
const result = await callAgent(
  'koda',
  'Build the complete subscription billing page with plan comparison',
  300000  // 5 minutes
)

// Fire and forget (don't await the result)
callAgent('mira', 'Extract lessons from today\'s Pinzo session')
```

**Error scenarios:**

The `success: false` result happens when:
1. Claude Hub is not reachable: `error` will be "Claude Hub not reachable at http://localhost:3847 — is it running?"
2. The call times out: `error` will be "Timed out after Xs"
3. Claude Hub returns a non-200 HTTP status
4. The `claude` CLI subprocess fails or returns an error event

### `listAgents()`

Fetches all available global agents from Claude Hub.

**Returns:** `Promise<Agent[]>`

```typescript

  description: string // description from frontmatter

### `isOnline()`

Checks if Claude Hub is reachable. Uses a 3-second timeout to avoid blocking.

**Returns:** `Promise<boolean>`

`true` if Claude Hub responds to `GET /api/global/agents` with a 200 status.
`false` if the request fails, times out, or returns a non-200 status.

**Example:**

```javascript
import { isOnline, callAgent } from '@boldteq/agents'

async function generateCopy(product: string) {
  if (!await isOnline()) {
    throw new Error('Claude Hub is offline. Start it with: pm2 start claude-hub')
  }
  return await callAgent('quill', `Write a tagline for ${product}`)
}
```

Use `isOnline()` as a guard when Claude Hub being offline would cause a bad user experience (e.g., a UI action that depends on agent output). For fire-and-forget calls (logging, async enrichment), just call the agent directly and handle the error in the result.

## Error Handling Patterns

### Pattern 1 — Simple check and log

```javascript
const result = await callAgent('quill', 'Write tagline')
if (!result.success) {
  console.error(`Agent failed: ${result.error}`)
  return null
}
return result.output
```

### Pattern 2 — Distinguish error types

```javascript
const result = await callAgent('koda', 'Build feature', 300000)

if (!result.success) {
  if (result.error?.includes('not reachable')) {
    // Claude Hub is down
    throw new Error('Claude Hub is offline. Run: pm2 start claude-hub')
  } else if (result.error?.includes('Timed out')) {
    // Task too complex for timeout — retry with longer timeout or smaller task
    const retry = await callAgent('koda', 'Build feature (simplified version)', 600000)
    return retry.success ? retry.output : null
  } else {
    // Agent ran but returned an error
    console.error('Agent error:', result.error)
    return null
  }
}

return result.output
```

### Pattern 3 — Guard with isOnline

```javascript
async function runAgentSafely(agent, prompt) {
  const online = await isOnline()
  if (!online) {
    return { success: false, output: '', agent, error: 'Claude Hub offline' }
  }
  return await callAgent(agent, prompt)
}
```

### 04-slash-commands.md
# Slash Commands — Complete Reference

This document covers everything about slash commands: what they are, how Claude Code discovers them, the `$ARGUMENTS` system, Pinzo's four commands in detail, and how to create new commands for any project.

---

## What Are Slash Commands?

Slash commands are `.md` files stored in `[project]/.claude/commands/`. When you type `/commandname` in Claude Code chat, it reads that file and executes its content as a prompt — with `$ARGUMENTS` replaced by whatever text follows the command name.

They are project-scoped workflow shortcuts. Instead of writing out the same detailed instructions every time you want to build a feature or run a review, you write them once in a command file and invoke them in one line.

### Example

Without a slash command:
> "Build a complete feature for Pinzo. Read CLAUDE.md first. Check Prisma schema. Handle auth. Use Polaris v13. Add empty states and loading states. Include Toast feedback for every mutation. Run typecheck when done. Report what was changed."

With a slash command:
> `/feature Add ZIP code import from CSV`

Same instructions, one line.

---

## How Slash Commands Differ from Agents

| | Agents | Slash Commands |
|-|--------|----------------|
| **Location** | `~/.claude/agents/` or `[project]/.claude/agents/` | `[project]/.claude/commands/` |
| **Scope** | Global or project | Project-only, always |
| **Invoked by** | Claude Code auto-routing, `@name`, SDK | You typing `/commandname` |
| **Has identity?** | Yes — name, model, description, persona | No — just instructions |
| **Purpose** | Specialist persona with persistent expertise | Repeatable workflow for one project |
| **Arguments?** | No — you describe the task in full | Yes — `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder |
| **Cost** | Uses agent's configured model | Uses current session model |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Use agents when you need Claude Code to automatically know about a specialist (Rex, Koda, Vex, etc.)
- Use slash commands for project-specific workflows you run manually and repeatedly (build feature, fix bug, run migration)

---

## How Claude Code Discovers Slash Commands

Claude Code scans `[project]/.claude/commands/` for `.md` files when the project is open. Each file's name (without `.md`) becomes the slash command name.

```
Pinzo/.claude/commands/
  feature.md    →  /feature
  fix.md        →  /fix
  review.md     →  /review
  db.md         →  /db
```

No registration needed. Create the file, and the command exists.

📝 Commands are project-scoped. `/feature` in Pinzo is not available when you have Rankora open. Each project has its own `.claude/commands/` directory.

📝 Command names are case-insensitive in practice but use lowercase by convention. Hyphens are fine: `/db-migrate`, `/release-notes`.

---

## The `$ARGUMENTS` Placeholder

`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced by everything the user types after the command name.

```
User types:  /feature Add CSV import for ZIP codes
$ARGUMENTS = "Add CSV import for ZIP codes"
```

The replacement is literal — the entire string, exactly as typed, including spaces. Claude Code does not parse or split the arguments.

### Using $ARGUMENTS in commands

```markdown
Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS

Read CLAUDE.md first. Build all layers from DB to UI.
```

When invoked as `/feature Add dark mode toggle`, the prompt becomes:
```
Build a complete feature for this project: Add dark mode toggle

Read CLAUDE.md first. Build all layers from DB to UI.
```

### Multiple uses of $ARGUMENTS

You can use `$ARGUMENTS` multiple times in one file. Each occurrence is replaced with the same string.

```markdown
## Task: $ARGUMENTS

You are implementing: $ARGUMENTS

Follow these steps...
```

### Commands without $ARGUMENTS

Some commands don't need arguments — they always do the same thing:

```markdown
Run a complete pre-deploy quality review of all recently modified files.

## Phase 1: Automated checks
Run npm run typecheck and npm run lint...
```

Invoke as just: `/review`

---

## Pinzo's Four Commands

Pinzo has the most complete slash command setup of any Boldteq project. These four commands cover the full development workflow.

### `/feature` — Build a Complete Feature

**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/feature.md`

**When to use:** Any time you want to add new functionality to Pinzo. This is the most-used command.

**What it does:**
1. Reads CLAUDE.md to understand the stack (React Router 7, Polaris v13, Prisma)
2. Reads 2+ existing route files to match code patterns exactly
3. Plans the feature (route type, models involved, data flow, billing gates)
4. Makes schema changes if needed (runs migrations)
5. Builds the route file with the correct auth pattern
6. Applies all Polaris v13 UI requirements (loading states, empty states, Toast feedback)
7. Runs `npm run typecheck` — zero tolerance for errors
8. Reports with file list, migration name, API endpoints, and test instructions

It routes work to project agents based on what's needed:
- New admin page → **builder** agent
- New/modified public API → **widget-specialist** agent
- Both needed → spawns them in parallel

**Usage:**
```
/feature Add product tagging to the admin dashboard
/feature Build a waitlist management page with bulk email notifications
/feature Add CSV import for ZIP codes with error reporting
/feature Create a delivery rules export as JSON
```

⚠️ Be specific in your argument. "Add something to the dashboard" will produce worse results than "Add a paginated delivery rules table with sort by priority, bulk delete, and CSV export."

---

### `/fix` — Diagnose and Fix a Bug

**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/fix.md`

**When to use:** Any error — TypeScript errors, runtime crashes, wrong data, Shopify auth failures, Prisma errors, webhook failures, billing bugs.

**What it does:**
1. Classifies the bug by category (auth, TypeScript, Polaris, DB, Shopify API, webhooks, billing)
2. Routes to the right agent based on category (bug-fixer for most, widget-specialist for widget/API issues)
3. Reads the full file where the error originates before touching anything
4. Makes the minimal, targeted fix — never refactors working code while fixing
5. Runs `npm run typecheck` to confirm zero errors
6. Reports root cause, files changed, and whether any follow-up is needed (migrations, env vars, etc.)

The command knows Pinzo's most common bugs:
- Auth missing on admin routes (70% of Shopify bugs)
- Missing `where: { shop: session.shop }` on DB queries
- Polaris v13 prop changes (`status` → `tone` in Badge/Banner)
- React Router 7 imports from wrong package (must be `react-router`, not `@remix-run/react`)
- Prisma unique constraint violations

**Usage:**
```
/fix TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined reading 'shop' in webhook handler
/fix npm run typecheck shows 3 errors in app/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
/fix The widget returns 404 for shops with apostrophes in their domain name
/fix Subscription status not updating after Shopify billing webhook fires
```

📝 Paste the exact error message as the argument. The more context the better. Stack traces, file names, and line numbers help a lot.

---

### `/review` — Quality Gate Before Shipping

**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/review.md`

**When to use:** After completing a feature or fix, before merging or deploying. This is the quality gate.

**What it does** (5 phases):

**Phase 1 — Automated checks:**
Runs `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint`. Reports results. Blocks the rest of the review if typecheck fails.

**Phase 2 — Security audit:**
Checks for: auth missing on admin routes, cross-shop data leaks (queries without `where: { shop: session.shop }`), public routes with accidental admin auth, exposed secrets in API responses, unsanitized input on public endpoints, missing CORS headers.

**Phase 3 — Shopify compliance:**
Checks for: Shopify API calls in components (must be in loaders/actions), raw fetch for Shopify API (must use `admin.graphql()`), missing idempotency in webhooks, raw HTML layout elements, missing loading/empty states/Toast feedback, ungated premium features.

**Phase 4 — Code quality:**
Checks for: TypeScript `any`, `console.log` in production code, TODO/FIXME comments, hardcoded values, wrong Remix imports, missing error handling.

**Phase 5 — API contract validation:**
If public APIs changed: verifies response shapes, status codes, CORS headers, and shop parameter validation.

The review outputs a structured report with critical issues (must fix), quality issues (should fix), and a final recommendation: SHIP IT / FIX CRITICAL FIRST / NEEDS REWORK.

**Usage:**
```
/review
/review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
/review after adding the waitlist feature
```

📝 `/review` with no arguments reviews all recently modified files (uses git diff). Pass a specific file to focus the review.

---

### `/db` — Database Workflows

**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/db.md`

**When to use:** Any time you need to change the Prisma schema, run migrations, optimize queries, or do bulk data operations.

**What it does:**
- For schema changes: reads current schema, plans the change, adds fields/models, runs `prisma migrate dev`, runs `prisma generate`, updates TypeScript references, runs typecheck
- For query optimization: analyzes existing queries, adds indexes, applies select/include optimization, uses transactions for multi-step operations
- For data operations: applies correct patterns (`upsert` for singletons, `createMany` for bulk, `$transaction` for multi-step)

It knows the full model catalog:
- **ZipCode** — `id, shop, zipCode, label, zone, message, eta, type` | unique: `[shop, zipCode]`
- **DeliveryRule** — `id, shop, name, zone, zipCodes, ...`
- **WaitlistEntry** — `id, shop, email, zipCode, status` | unique: `[shop, email, zipCode]`
- **WidgetConfig** — singleton per shop | unique: `shop`
- **Subscription** — singleton per shop | unique: `shop`
- **Session** — Shopify-managed, NEVER modify

It also handles the SQLite (dev) vs PostgreSQL (prod) differences.

**Usage:**
```
/db Add index on orders.shop for query performance
/db Add a notes field to WaitlistEntry
/db Create a new ProductTag model linked to shop
/db Optimize the zip code lookup query for high-volume stores
/db Add analytics tracking fields to Subscription
```

⚠️ `/db` will NEVER run `prisma migrate reset` without explicit confirmation — this deletes all data. If you accidentally type it, the command will ask you to confirm and explain the consequences.

---

## Creating Slash Commands for Your Own Workflow

### Step 1 — Understand what the command needs to do

Write down in one sentence what this command's job is. "This command builds a complete feature for this project, handling all layers and quality gates." If you can't describe it in one sentence, it might need to be two commands.

### Step 2 — Create the file

```bash
touch "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/YourProject/.claude/commands/feature.md"
```

The filename (without `.md`) is the command name.

### Step 3 — Write the command

```markdown
Build a complete feature for this project: $ARGUMENTS

## Context
Read CLAUDE.md first to understand the stack and architecture.
Read at least 2 existing files that are similar to what you're building to match code patterns.

## Process
1. Plan the feature (what files, what data, what APIs)
2. Make any schema changes first (if using a DB)
3. Build the implementation
4. Apply all quality standards (types, error handling, loading states)
5. Run the type checker — fix every error
6. Report: files changed, how to test, what to do next

## Standards from CLAUDE.md apply. Read it before building.
```

### Naming conventions

- Lowercase only: `feature`, `fix`, `review`, `db`
- Hyphens for multi-word: `db-migrate`, `release-notes`, `type-check`
- Short: you type these often. `feature` not `build-complete-feature`
- One command per workflow: don't make `/feature-admin` and `/feature-api` separately — make one `/feature` that handles both

### Best practices for command content

**Always include:**
- What stack/framework this command is for (reference CLAUDE.md)
- Which agent to route to (if the command delegates to a specialist)
- What quality gates must pass before the task is "done"
- What the output/report format should be

**The more specific, the better:**
```markdown
Bad:  Build a feature: $ARGUMENTS
Good: Build a complete Shopify admin page for: $ARGUMENTS
      - Use React Router 7 with Polaris v13
      - Include authenticate.admin in loader and action
      - Add SkeletonPage loading state
      - Add EmptyState for empty lists
      - Add Toast for every mutation
      - Run npm run typecheck — zero tolerance
```

**Define "done" explicitly:**
The command should tell Claude Code exactly what state the code must be in before it reports completion. "Run the type checker and fix every error" is a quality gate. Without it, Claude might report done while there are still TypeScript errors.

---

## Creating Commands That Wrap Global Agents

A powerful pattern: a slash command that provides project context to a global agent, so you don't have to type the context every time.

### Why this is useful

Without the pattern:
```
@sage Review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx. This is a Shopify app using React Router 7 and Polaris v13. Check for missing auth, cross-shop data leaks, Polaris v13 compliance, etc.
```

With the pattern (a `/review` command that calls sage):
```
/review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx
```

The command file provides all the Pinzo-specific context to Sage, so you only need to provide the specific file.

### Template

```markdown
<!-- .claude/commands/review.md -->
Review the following for this project: $ARGUMENTS

## Project Context
This is the Pinzo Shopify app:
- Framework: React Router 7
- UI: Polaris v13
- Auth: authenticate.admin() from shopify.server.ts
- DB: Prisma with shop-scoped queries

## What to review (route this to sage):
1. Security: auth missing, cross-shop leaks, exposed secrets
2. Shopify compliance: API calls in components, wrong imports
3. Polaris v13 compliance: loading states, empty states, Toast
4. TypeScript: no any, all functions typed
5. Code quality: error handling, console.logs, TODOs

## Report format:
- Critical issues (must fix before shipping)
- Quality issues (should fix)
- Recommendation: SHIP IT / FIX CRITICAL / NEEDS REWORK
```

### Examples for wrapping each global agent

**`/quill` — generate copy with project context:**
```markdown
<!-- .claude/commands/quill.md -->
Generate content for this Shopify app: $ARGUMENTS

## Project context for Quill:
- App name: Pinzo
- What it does: Shopify ZIP code delivery eligibility checker
- Tone: Clear, direct, conversion-focused
- Brand: Professional, reliable, merchant-friendly

Write copy that matches this brand voice.
```

**`/nova` — research with project focus:**
```markdown
<!-- .claude/commands/nova.md -->
Research this topic for Pinzo development: $ARGUMENTS

## Context:
We're building Pinzo — a Shopify ZIP code delivery restriction app.
Focus research on: Shopify app ecosystem, merchant pain points, delivery use cases.
Return: competitive analysis, feature opportunities, pricing insights.
```

---

## Commands vs Agents: Decision Guide

| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| You do the same workflow in this project more than once a week | Slash command |
| The workflow is always the same but the subject changes | Slash command with `$ARGUMENTS` |
| You need Claude Code to automatically route to a specialist | Agent |
| The specialist's expertise spans multiple projects | Global agent |
| The specialist is deeply tied to one project's code | Project agent |
| You want to invoke logic programmatically from Node code | Agent via SDK |
| You want to invoke it from the chat interface by typing | Slash command |

When in doubt: create a slash command. They're easier to write and test than agents, and they're directly invocable by you without needing to describe the task in full every time.

### 05-orchestration.md
# Agent Orchestration — Complete Reference

This document covers everything about the Orchestration feature in Claude Hub: what it is, when to use it, how to build pipelines, the execution engine, advanced patterns, and troubleshooting.

---

## What Is Orchestration?

Orchestration is a visual workflow system inside Claude Hub that lets you chain multiple Claude agents together as a directed graph (DAG). Each node in the graph runs one agent or custom step. The output of each node automatically flows into the next node as context.

You define the pipeline once. Then you give it a top-level task and run it. Each agent handles one stage: researching, planning, building, reviewing. The whole pipeline executes without you manually passing output from one agent to the next.

### The simplest possible orchestration

```
[Task Input] → Nova (research) → Quill (draft)
```

1. You type: "Write App Store listing for Pinzo"
2. Nova researches Pinzo and similar apps, returns competitor analysis and key angles
3. Quill receives Nova's research as context and writes the App Store listing using it

Nova's output becomes Quill's input automatically. You didn't have to copy-paste anything.

---

## When to Use Orchestration vs Other Approaches

| Situation | Best approach |
|-----------|--------------|
| Quick one-off task | Ask Claude Code directly in chat |
| Repeatable single-agent workflow | Slash command |
| Multi-step task with distinct specialist phases | Orchestration |
| Task where later stages need earlier stages' output | Orchestration |
| You want to test different pipeline structures | Orchestration |
| Programmatic agent calls from code | SDK (`callAgent`) |
| Interactive back-and-forth conversation | Claude Code chat |

Orchestration is best when you have 2+ stages that require different expertise and where later stages genuinely benefit from earlier stages' output. If all stages can be done by one agent or don't need context from each other, use a slash command instead.

---

## How the Visual Canvas Works

### Opening Orchestration

1. Open http://localhost:3847
2. Click **Orchestration** in the left sidebar

You land on the canvas. It has:
- A blank canvas area (main working area)
- A sidebar on the right for node configuration
- A Run panel at the bottom
- A toolbar at the top with: New, Save, templates, node palette

### Nodes

Every pipeline is made of nodes. Each node represents one step.

**Node types:**

| Type | Description | Claude call? |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| Start / Task Input | The initial prompt. Pass-through — no agent runs. | No |
| Agent Node | Runs a global agent (Nova, Quill, Koda, etc.) with an optional instruction override | Yes |
| Custom Step | Runs Claude with instructions you write entirely yourself | Yes |

**Node anatomy:**
- **Label** — the display name on the canvas (e.g., "Research", "Draft", "Polish")
- **Agent** (Agent nodes only) — which agent from `~/.claude/agents/` to use
- **Instructions** — what to tell this agent/step. This overrides or supplements the agent's default behavior for this specific step.

### Edges

Edges are arrows connecting nodes. They define the flow:
- Draw an arrow from Node A to Node B → Node B receives Node A's output as context
- Draw multiple arrows into Node B → Node B receives all upstream outputs, labeled by source
- A node with no incoming edges starts with the original task as its context

### The DAG constraint

The graph must be a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — no cycles. You cannot connect Node C back to Node A if A → B → C. The execution engine uses topological sort, which requires no cycles. If you add a circular edge, the system rejects it.

Valid graphs:
```
Linear:      A → B → C
Fan-out:     A → B
             A → C
Fan-in:      B → D
             C → D
Combined:    A → B → D → E
             A → C → D
```

---

## The Execution Engine

### What happens when you click Run

**Phase 1 — Graph validation:**
- Receives the node list and edge list from the frontend
- Builds a node map for fast lookup
- Detects cycles (rejects if found)
- Performs topological sort to determine execution order
- Ensures dependencies are respected (no node runs before its inputs are ready)

**Phase 2 — Load agents:**
- Reads all `.md` files from `~/.claude/agents/`
- Reads `.md` files from each project's `.claude/agents/`
- Builds a map: agentName → full system prompt

**Phase 3 — Sequential execution:**

For each node in topological order:

1. If it's a start/task node: store the original task as its output, emit `{ type: 'start' }` + `{ type: 'done' }` events, move on. No Claude call made.

2. If it's an agent or custom node:
   - Emit `{ type: 'start', nodeId, label }` → the canvas shows this node as "running" (purple animation)
   - Collect outputs from all upstream nodes
   - Build context string:
     ```
     ## Output from [Upstream Node A label]:
     [Node A's output]
     
     ## Output from [Upstream Node B label]:
     [Node B's output]
     ```
   - Build full prompt:
     ```
     [Agent system prompt or custom instructions]
     
     ---
     
     [Context from upstream nodes]
     
     Provide your response:
     ```
   - Run `claude -p "[full prompt]"` as a subprocess
   - Wait for subprocess to complete (120-second timeout)
   - Store the output
   - Emit `{ type: 'done', nodeId, label, output }` → canvas shows green checkmark

3. After all nodes: emit `{ type: 'complete', finalOutput }` → Run panel shows final result

**Phase 4 — SSE streaming:**

The frontend receives real-time updates via Server-Sent Events. The node statuses change live as execution proceeds:
- `idle` → gray (before run)
- `running` → animated purple (executing now)
- `done` → green with checkmark
- `error` → red with error icon

---

## Context Passing: How Upstream Outputs Become Downstream Inputs

This is the key mechanism. Understanding it helps you write better pipelines.

### Single upstream (linear chain)

Node B receives output from Node A:

```
Full prompt sent to Node B:
═══════════════════════════════
[Node B's instructions]

---

## Output from Research:
[Everything Nova returned]

Provide your response:
═══════════════════════════════
```

Node B's Claude call sees Node A's full output as context. It can reference, summarize, or build on it.

### Multiple upstream (fan-in)

Node D receives from both Node B and Node C:

```
Full prompt sent to Node D:
═══════════════════════════════
[Node D's instructions]

---

## Output from Planner:
[Everything the Planner node returned]

## Output from Researcher:
[Everything the Researcher node returned]

Provide your response:
═══════════════════════════════
```

Node D's Claude call sees both outputs, clearly labeled. It can synthesize them, compare them, or use them independently.

### Real example: Research → Draft → Polish

```
Task: "Write App Store listing for Pinzo"

Node 1 (Start): passes "Write App Store listing for Pinzo" as output

Node 2 (Nova — Research):
  Receives: "Write App Store listing for Pinzo"
  Instructions: "Research Shopify ZIP code apps. Find top competitors, their listings, weak points."
  Output: "Top competitors: ZipSeller ($9.99/mo, weak onboarding), DeliveryFilter ($14.99, no analytics)..."

Node 3 (Quill — Draft):
  Receives: Node 2's full research output
  Instructions: "Write a Shopify App Store listing draft. Use the research to position against competitors."
  Output: "Pinzo — Smart Delivery Zone Control\n\nKnow exactly where you can deliver..."

Node 4 (Quill — Polish):
  Receives: Node 3's draft
  Instructions: "Polish this listing. Tighten every sentence. Remove filler. Ensure first 2 sentences hook."
  Output: [final polished listing]
```

---

## Building Your First Pipeline (Step by Step)

### Goal: Research → Write → Polish for any content piece

This is the default template. Here's how to build it from scratch.

**Step 1 — Open the canvas**

Click **Orchestration** → **New** (or use the built-in template by clicking the template name from the list).

**Step 2 — Add the Start node**

Every pipeline needs a Start node. It's the entry point for your task input.
- Click the canvas to add a node (or use the node palette)
- Select type: **Start / Task Input**
- Label: "Task Input"

**Step 3 — Add the Research node**

- Add a node
- Type: **Agent Node**
- Agent: **Nova**
- Label: "Research"
- Instructions: "Research the given topic. Find competitors, key angles, user pain points. Return structured findings with bullet points."

Connect: Task Input → Research (draw an arrow)

**Step 4 — Add the Draft node**

- Add a node
- Type: **Agent Node**
- Agent: **Quill**
- Label: "Draft"
- Instructions: "Using the research provided, write a complete first draft. Be specific, benefit-focused. Do not use generic filler."

Connect: Research → Draft

**Step 5 — Add the Polish node**

- Add a node
- Type: **Agent Node**
- Agent: **Quill**
- Label: "Polish"
- Instructions: "Polish this draft. Tighten every sentence. Cut filler words. Ensure the opening hooks immediately. Return the final polished version only — no commentary."

## Node Instructions: Bad vs Good

This is the most important thing to get right. Bad node instructions produce bad or empty output.

### The root problem

If node instructions say "analyze this" without specifying what to produce, Claude might:
- Ask clarifying questions instead of producing output
- Return a meta-commentary about what it would do, rather than doing it
- Produce the right content but buried in unnecessary explanation

**Bad node instructions:**
```
Analyze the research and think about what content would work best.
```
Claude will describe what good content looks like, not write it.

**Good node instructions:**
```
You are a Shopify app copywriter. Using the research provided:
1. Identify the top 3 user pain points mentioned
2. Write a 5-bullet feature list that directly addresses those pain points
3. Write a 150-word app description

Return the bullets and description only. No commentary.
```
Claude has a clear role, a clear input, clear output requirements, and explicit format.

### The explicit output format rule

Every node instruction should specify:
1. **What format to return** ("Return a bullet list", "Return only the code", "Return a structured JSON object")
2. **What NOT to include** ("No commentary", "No preamble", "No explanation")
3. **Length or scope** ("150 words", "5 bullets", "complete implementation")

Without these, agents often return meta-content (explaining what they're doing) rather than the deliverable itself.

### More examples

**Bad — Planner node:**
```
Think about the task and break it down.
```

**Good — Planner node:**
```
Break the given task into 5 or fewer concrete implementation steps.
Number each step. Be specific: mention file names, method names, and data types where relevant.
Return the numbered list only.
```

**Bad — Code reviewer:**
```
Review the code.
```

**Good — Code reviewer:**
```
You are a TypeScript code reviewer.
Check for:
1. Missing type annotations
2. Unsafe type assertions or `any` usage
3. Unhandled promise rejections
4. Missing error boundaries

Output format:
## Issues Found
- [severity: critical/warning] [file/line]: [problem] → [fix]

## Verdict: PASS / NEEDS FIXES
```

## Advanced Patterns

### Pattern 1: Fan-Out (Multi-Perspective Research)

Use when you want multiple independent perspectives on the same topic before synthesizing.

```
Task Input
  → Researcher A: "Find solutions in TypeScript/Node"
  → Researcher B: "Find solutions in Python approaches"
  → Synthesizer: "Compare approaches, recommend best for our stack"
  → Developer: "Implement the recommended approach"
```

Both Researcher A and B receive only the task. Synthesizer receives both their outputs. Developer receives Synthesizer's recommendation.

**When to use:** Architecture decisions, technical comparisons, multi-angle analysis.

### Pattern 2: Plan → Implement → Validate

A three-stage code generation pipeline.

```
Task Input → Planner (Arya) → Developer (Koda) → Reviewer (Sage)
```

Arya breaks the task into a build plan. Koda implements from the plan. Sage reviews Koda's implementation.

**When to use:** Complex feature builds where you want architecture thought through before coding.

### Pattern 3: Summarizer Nodes for Long Context

Problem: Node 1 outputs 8KB of research. Node 2 outputs 12KB of code. Node 3 receives 20KB of context — slow, expensive, risks hitting limits.

Solution: Add a Summarizer node between steps.

```
Research → Summarizer (100 words max) → Developer
```

Summarizer instruction:
```
Condense the above research into 5 key bullet points. 
Maximum 100 words total. 
Preserve the most actionable insights.
```

The Developer then works with 100 words of targeted context instead of 8KB of raw research.

### Pattern 4: Cascading Specialization

```
Task (general) → Planner (breaks into sub-tasks) → Specialist A (sub-task 1) → Specialist B (sub-task 2) → Integrator (combines)
```

Each specialist receives: the original task + Planner's output + their specific part to handle.
The Integrator receives: all specialist outputs and synthesizes them.

**When to use:** Building multiple distinct components that need to work together. Example: "Build the pricing page" → Planner splits into (a) pricing logic, (b) UI layout, (c) copy. Koda handles logic and layout in parallel (conceptually). Quill handles copy. Final node integrates.

### Pattern 5: Validation Gate

```
Task → Developer → Validator → (done if valid, re-run with feedback if not)
```

Validator instruction:
```
Review the code above. Check:
1. Does it compile? (TypeScript syntax check)
2. Does it follow the project patterns?
3. Are error handling and loading states present?

Output:
## PASS / FAIL
If FAIL, list: [issue] → [required fix]
```

If Validator outputs FAIL, you can see exactly what needs fixing and re-run with adjusted Developer instructions that address the Validator's feedback.

## Performance Considerations

### Timing

| Operation | Typical time |
|-----------|-------------|
| Start/Task node | < 1ms (no Claude call) |
| Simple agent step (short task) | 5–20 seconds |
| Complex agent step (full implementation) | 20–60 seconds |
| Full 3-node pipeline | 30–90 seconds |
| Full 5-node pipeline | 75–180 seconds |

Every node makes exactly one `claude -p` subprocess call. Nodes execute sequentially — not in parallel.

### How to keep pipelines fast

1. **Limit context size** — use summarizer nodes between heavy output nodes
2. **Focused instructions** — specific instructions = faster, better output
3. **Appropriate agent for each step** — Sonnet is faster than Opus. Use Opus only for Arya/Sage/Rex nodes.
4. **Don't chain more nodes than needed** — 3–5 nodes is the sweet spot. 7+ nodes is usually overkill.
5. **Break into multiple smaller pipelines** — instead of one 8-node monster, run two 4-node pipelines sequentially

## Troubleshooting

### Node turns red / error

**Symptom:** A node shows a red error icon during a run.

**Cause A — Timeout:** The node took longer than 120 seconds.

Fix:
- Click the failed node to see the error message
- Simplify the instructions (break the task into smaller pieces)
- Or split the node into two nodes with focused responsibilities

**Cause B — Claude CLI error:** The `claude` subprocess returned an error.

Fix:
```bash
# Verify claude CLI works manually
claude -p "Say hello" --print
# If this fails, the CLI has a problem — re-authenticate:
claude login
```

**Cause C — Empty output:** The node ran but returned nothing useful.

Fix: The instructions likely don't direct Claude to produce a concrete deliverable. See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" above.

---

### Circular edge detected

**Symptom:** System shows error "Circular dependency detected" when you try to run.

**Cause:** You connected nodes in a way that creates a loop (A → B → C → A).

**Fix:** Find and remove the circular edge. The system highlights the problematic edge in red. Delete it. Orchestration only supports DAGs (no cycles).

---

### Disconnected nodes

**Symptom:** A node never runs — it stays gray after the run completes.

**Cause:** The node has no incoming edges and is not a Start node. It's isolated from the graph.

**Fix:** Connect the node to at least one other node. Either draw an edge from a preceding node to it, or delete it if it's not needed.

---

### Output is meta-commentary instead of content

**Symptom:** A node returns "I would write the listing like this: [description of the listing]" instead of the actual listing.

**Cause:** Node instructions don't specify that the agent should produce the deliverable directly.

**Fix:** Add explicit output format instructions:
```
Write the listing. Return the listing only. No preamble, no commentary, no explanation.
```

See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" for more examples.

---

### Context ballooning (slow pipeline)

**Symptom:** Later nodes in the pipeline are very slow or timing out.

**Cause:** Upstream nodes produced large outputs that all get passed as context to downstream nodes. By node 4 or 5, the context is 20KB+ of text.

**Fix:** Add a Summarizer node:
```
Node 3 (long output) → Summarizer ("Condense to 5 key points, max 200 words") → Node 4
```

---

### Save not persisting

**Symptom:** You save a pipeline, close Claude Hub, reopen it, and the pipeline is gone.

**Cause:** Write permission issue on `orchestrations.json`.

**Fix:**
```bash
ls -l "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
# If not writable:
chmod 644 "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
```

---

### SSE events not streaming (run panel shows nothing)

**Symptom:** You click Run, nothing happens in the run panel. After a long wait, maybe an error appears.

**Cause:** The SSE connection between the frontend and backend is broken. Often caused by a proxy or browser extension interrupting the connection.

**Fix:**
1. Check Claude Hub logs: `pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 30`
2. Look for errors in the browser console (F12 → Console)
3. Try a hard reload: Cmd+Shift+R
4. If pm2 shows errors: `pm2 restart claude-hub` then reload the page

# Adding a New Project to the Boldteq System

This guide covers everything you need to do when starting a new project or onboarding an existing one. By the end, Claude Code will know about the project, your agents will have context, slash commands will be available, and the SDK will be wired up.

---

## Why Setup Matters

A new project without proper setup means:
- Claude Code has no knowledge of the stack, patterns, or decisions
- No repeatable commands — you re-explain the same workflow every session
- No SDK access — you can't call agents programmatically
- Claude Hub doesn't know the project exists — no dashboard, no agent management

A properly setup project means:
- Claude Code opens with full context on the first message
- `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review` work immediately
- `callAgent('koda', 'build X')` works from any script
- The project appears in Claude Hub with all agents and commands visible

## Step 1 — Create the Project's CLAUDE.md

### Why this matters

The project-level `CLAUDE.md` at the project root is read by Claude Code when that project is open. It supplements the global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` with project-specific context: exact stack versions, folder structure, architecture decisions, and patterns specific to this codebase.

Without it, Claude Code builds on generic assumptions. With it, Claude Code knows exactly what `authenticate.admin(request)` means, what your Prisma models look like, and what your quality standards are.

### Required sections

Every project CLAUDE.md must have:

```markdown
# [Project Name] — [Type: Shopify App / SaaS / API]

- Framework: [exact name and version]
- UI: [UI library and version]
- Auth: [how auth works]
- Database: [ORM + DB]
- Language: TypeScript everywhere — zero plain .js files
- Bundler: [if applicable]
- Node: [minimum version]

## Folder Structure
\`\`\`
[Show the actual top-level directories and key files]
\`\`\`

## Architecture Rules
[5–10 explicit rules about how code must be written]
1. [Rule]
2. [Rule]
...

## UI Rules
[If there's a UI library — what components to use, what's forbidden]

## Database Models
[If using a DB — list all models with key fields]

## Route Patterns
[If using file-based routing — show the pattern table]

## Quality Gates
[What must pass before any code is considered done]
- npm run typecheck — zero errors
- [project-specific checks]
```

**Fix:**

```bash

# If it returns a PID (e.g., 12345), kill it

# If no PID returned but error persists, wait 5 seconds and try again

# Now start
pm2 restart claude-hub
# or
cd "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub"
npm start
```

## Orchestration Issues

### Symptom: Node produces meta-commentary instead of the actual deliverable

**Example:** Quill node returns "I would write the App Store listing as follows: [describes what a good listing looks like]" instead of the actual listing.

**Cause:** Node instructions don't explicitly direct the agent to produce the deliverable.

**Fix:** Update the node's instructions to include:
- An explicit "produce this" directive
- Output format specification
- "No commentary, no preamble, no explanation" instruction

```
Before: "Think about what would make a good App Store listing"
After:  "Write the App Store listing. Return only the listing text — title, subtitle, description, feature bullets. No commentary."
```

---

### Symptom: Orchestration run times out on a node

```
Node execution timed out after 120s
```

**Cause:** The node's task is too complex for the 120-second limit.

**Fix options:**

1. Simplify the node's instructions (narrower scope)
2. Split into two nodes (Plan node → Execute node)
3. Break one big task into smaller parallel branches that each take less time

---

### Symptom: "Circular dependency detected" error

**Cause:** You connected nodes in a cycle (A → B → C → A).

**Fix:** Find and remove the circular edge. The system highlights it. Delete the edge that closes the loop.

Valid flow: A → B → C (linear, fine)
Invalid flow: A → B → C → A (circular, rejected)

---

### Symptom: A node never runs (stays gray after run completes)

**Cause:** The node is disconnected — no incoming edges.

**Fix:** Connect the node to at least one upstream node. Or delete it if it's not needed.

---

### Symptom: Later nodes run before their inputs are ready

This shouldn't happen (the topological sort prevents it), but if it does:

**Cause:** A node has edges but they're not pointing in the right direction (arrow is going the wrong way).

**Fix:** Delete the edge and redraw it in the correct direction. Arrows should flow from earlier stages to later stages.

## What Is This System?

The Boldteq Software Factory is a local AI-powered development infrastructure that runs on your Mac. It turns Claude Code (the VS Code extension) from a general-purpose assistant into a coordinated team of 12 specialist agents that know your stack, your standards, and your active projects.

Every component in this system has one job. They are designed to work together without requiring you to repeat context.

---

## The Five Components

### 1. Claude Hub — The Control Center

**Location:** `/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/`

Claude Hub is a local web application running on `http://localhost:3847`. It has two parts:

- **Express backend** (`src/server.js`) — REST API that reads/writes agent files, CLAUDE.md files, slash commands, and handles orchestration runs and playground agent calls.
- **React/TypeScript/Vite frontend** (`client/`) — The browser dashboard you use to manage everything.

Claude Hub is kept alive 24/7 by pm2 and auto-starts on macOS login via a LaunchAgent. You never manually start it.

Pages in the dashboard:
- **Dashboard** — overview of all projects, agents, and commands
- **All Agents** — browse and edit all 12 global agents
- **All Commands** — browse slash commands across all projects
- **Orchestration** — visual DAG workflow builder for chaining agents
- **Playground** — test any single agent interactively
- **Global CLAUDE.md** — view and edit the global instruction file
- **Project Detail** — per-project agents, commands, and CLAUDE.md
- **Setup & Status** — system health, SDK installer, project directories
- **Settings** — project directory configuration

### 2. Global CLAUDE.md — The Briefing File

**Location:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`

Every single Claude Code session in every project reads this file first. It contains the Boldteq identity, build standards, agent routing rules, and active project list. It is the foundation that makes Claude Code behave consistently across all projects. Without it, Claude Code has no knowledge of your stack, agents, or standards.

### 3. The Agent Roster — The Specialist Team

**Location:** `~/.claude/agents/`

12 `.md` files, each one a specialist persona with a name, model, and system prompt. Claude Code loads all of them at startup and can route tasks to the right specialist automatically. You can also invoke them explicitly by name. The agents cover the entire build lifecycle from research to deployment to monitoring.

### 4. The SDK — Programmatic Agent Access

**Location:** `claude-hub/sdk/` (installed as `@boldteq/agents` in each project)

A tiny Node.js package that lets any project call any agent over HTTP with one line of code. It posts to Claude Hub which runs `claude -p` with the agent's instructions and streams back the result. Zero cost beyond the existing Claude subscription.

### 5. Slash Commands — Repeatable Workflows

**Location:** `[project]/.claude/commands/`

`.md` files that become `/commandname` shortcuts in Claude Code chat. Pinzo has `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review`, and `/db`. These are pre-written, detailed instructions for the most common workflows in that project. You type the command, pass arguments, and Claude Code executes the full workflow.

## Step 4 — Set Up pm2 (Permanent Background Service)

### Why pm2?

Without pm2, Claude Hub only runs while your terminal is open. Close the terminal → Claude Hub stops → SDK calls fail → Playground stops working → Orchestration stops working.

pm2 is a process manager that:
- Runs Claude Hub as a background daemon (no terminal needed)
- Automatically restarts it if it crashes
- Persists across terminal sessions
- Starts automatically after a system reboot (when combined with LaunchAgent)
- Gives you logging, monitoring, and process control

## Step 5 — LaunchAgent Setup (Auto-Start on macOS Login)

### Why a LaunchAgent?

pm2 manages the process, but pm2 itself needs to be started after a reboot. The LaunchAgent is macOS's built-in service system. It runs a specified program when you log in, before you open any apps.

Without a LaunchAgent:
- After a Mac restart, pm2 is not running
- Claude Hub is not running
- The SDK fails silently in all projects
- You must manually run `pm2 resurrect` or `pm2 start ecosystem.config.js` after every reboot

With the LaunchAgent:
- Mac restarts → login → LaunchAgent fires → `node src/server.js` starts → Claude Hub is running → all SDK calls work

📝 Note: The LaunchAgent in this setup runs Claude Hub **directly** (not via pm2). This is intentional — it guarantees Claude Hub starts even if pm2's process list was lost.

### Check if the plist already exists

```bash
ls ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist
```

Expected: path printed (file exists).

If missing, you need to create it. See "Creating the plist from scratch" below.

### The full plist content

The file at `~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist` should contain:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>io.boldteq.claude-hub</string>

  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin/node</string>
    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/src/server.js</string>
  </array>

  <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub</string>

  <key>RunAtLoad</key>
  <true/>

  <key>KeepAlive</key>
  <true/>

  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-launchd.log</string>

  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-launchd-error.log</string>

  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
  <dict>
    <key>PORT</key>
    <string>3847</string>
    <key>PATH</key>
    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin</string>
  </dict>
</dict>
</plist>
```

Each key explained:
- `Label` — unique identifier for this LaunchAgent. Used with `launchctl`.
- `ProgramArguments` — the exact command to run. First element is the Node binary path, second is the script. Must use absolute paths.
- `WorkingDirectory` — the directory node runs from. Must match the `cwd` in ecosystem.config.js.
- `RunAtLoad: true` — start immediately when the LaunchAgent is loaded (at login).
- `KeepAlive: true` — macOS will restart the process if it exits. Like pm2's autorestart.
- `StandardOutPath` / `StandardErrorPath` — log files. Reuses the pm2 log directory for convenience.
- `EnvironmentVariables` — sets PORT and PATH so the Node process can find other tools (like `claude`).

⚠️ The Node binary path (`/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin/node`) must be exact. If you switch Node versions or use a different installation method, update this path. Find yours with:
```bash
which node
```

**Cause:** Another process is using port 3847. Either a previous Claude Hub instance is still running, or something else claimed the port.

**Fix:**
```bash
# Find what's using the port
lsof -ti:3847

# If it returns a PID, kill it
kill -9 $(lsof -ti:3847)

# Now start Claude Hub
pm2 restart claude-hub
# or
npm start
```
